content: Partial formalization (33k+ lines up to Golod-Shafarevich) announced by Logical Intelligence. A previous partial formalization existed according to my reading of a post by Daniel Litt, and it's unclear whether this is more complete.

@Tanner Duve, to be honest, I am pretty disappointed by the framing of Logical Intelligence's announcement here. The fact that I have to scroll two pages through the blog post before there is any admission that the proof relies on axioms is really not okay, and, for me at least, really poisons your achievement.

It's a great achievement! Why sully it by such misleading framing?
(There's a lean-eval problem for this: https://lean-lang.org/eval/problems/erdos_unit_distance_conjecture_false/, which of course remains unsolved.)

Even "up to" is ambiguous -- I read "formalization up to Golod-Shafarevich" as meaning "we did the amazing job of formalizing everything up until the proof of Golod-Shafarevich, what's left is the new work" not what it actually means, which is "we skipped the hard part".

I think that we should be actively encouraging people (and companies) to publish more proofs-with-axioms-left-in, as Kim points out, it's still a "great achievement". I much prefer a world where this is the norm and we see new papers getting verified modulo standard results, over slop proofs that take nonsensical definitions to sneakily sidestep the hard part. Preferably also with some cultural standard like, "we asked two experienced Mathlib contributors from this domain to check that our sorried claims looked correct and they were being used in plausible ways".

This is part of why alarm bells go off in my head so strong when announcement says "zero axioms, zero sorries" (besides the fact that Claude seems to have just memorizes this phrase). It seems like only humans like to leave axioms. :)

note as well that multiple mathlib maintainers were consulted to review the formalizations of the stated assumptions, which were stated and used as hypotheses in the final proof, not declared as global axioms. the assumptions were stated explicitly in the (short) article.

Yes, it's great that you did this review, and that further down in the blog post you clearly explain this!

What's unacceptable is that this information is hidden two pages into the announcements.

But I want to push back against Alex's claim that we should publish more proofs-with-axioms-left-in.

If you come up with the axioms yourselves, then it's bullshit, and a waste of time, and distracting the community's resources, to publish results modulo those axioms. Sorry.

If those "axioms" are already published somewhere independently of your project, and reviewed as part of a roadmap towards actually filling in the "axioms" in public libraries, then great, awesome, we can all be on the same page.

(To be honest I am actually somewhat disappointed that Johan and Kevin bothered to review these holes in the proof. I was asked at the same time, and refused. I said instead: if you would like to publish the gaps that you think you need, I would be happy to consider including them in lean-eval so we can get some review and stress testing of the gaps --- and I would prefer that there were better mechanisms than that one.)
10 messages were moved here from #Machine Learning for Theorem Proving > OpenAI with a shiny new claim : the unit distance problem by Kim Morrison.
Yes, zero sorries matters far less than zero hidden trust boundaries.

This one page disproof doesn't use class field theory and might be within reach of Aristotle ...

ok, i guess i’ll unit distance poast one last time. amusingly this one found a counterexample without any serious number theoretic input, i.e. no class field towers, just intro number theory stuff. you just adjoin square roots of the first many negative prime discriminants (erdos’s \Q(i) construction being the first case) and consider an exponentially longer product of primes congruent to 1 mod 4, pigeonhole to get a lot of ideal divisors in the same ideal class, and then it’s the same rescaling construction as erdos. this doesn’t gain a power, “just” disproves the conjecture, so i hadn’t shared it before, but i thought people might enjoy because of the lack of inputs.
surely no surprise to my oai friends either of course! but it shows one needn’t have had class field theory to have disproved the thing. and it’s (arguably) a one-liner!

Finished in https://github.com/kim-em/erdos-unit-distance

Is that the first end-to-end formalization of the negation of the unit distance conjecture?

Fun. Fable+Codex+Aristotle is a pretty capable combination: I had zero involvement here, I never even opened the PDF.
There's a #formalization.yaml file, of course: https://github.com/kim-em/erdos-unit-distance/blob/master/formalization.yaml
Fun fact: the lean-eval problem as stated is the "stronger than the negation: we actually achieve some specific super-linear power" version, so this proof doesn't suffice to do that.
